Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 240 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2020) 
 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 240 is located in east-central Alberta within the Red Deer-North Saskatchewan 
Region. The unit is approximately 1371 km2. The Vermilion River runs through the centre area of the unit, with 
Waskwei Creek in the northwest. The unit is mostly agricultural, with cultivation dominating in the west and more 
grazing in the east. Native habitat is dominated by aspen parkland, with some native  grassland. 
 
The most recent previous aerial ungulate survey conducted in this unit used the strip transect survey method and 
was conducted in 2013. Results of previous surveys are summarized in Tables 1-3. 
 
The objective of the survey conducted in January 2020 was to assess the status of the ungulate population in this 
WMU by determining estimates of population size, density and age-sex composition. We also recorded 
observations of additional species of interest, including carnivores, game birds, and sensitive or species at risk.  
 
Survey Method 
 
From January 23-24, 2020, a strip transect survey was conducted flying north-south lines at 1.6 km (1 mile) 
intervals resulting in 25% coverage (with 400 m wide survey strip) for a total linear survey effort of 841 km (337 
km2). Snow conditions were good, with some hoar frost on one morning. At each observation point, ungulates were 
counted by species, and, when possible, classified by sex and age. 
 
Sex and age classification was determined for moose by identification of vulva patch and size differential of 
cow/calves. Sex and age classification was determined for deer using antlers and size differential between adults and 
fawns. Density was calculated for white-tailed deer, mule deer and moose following Jolly 1969 (as described in 
Krebs 2014) for surveys conducted with unequal sized units without replacement because the  transect lengths 
varied. Density was multiplied by the WMU area to determine population estimates. 90% confidence intervals were 
also calculated. A correction factor of 83% for deer detectability was applied to population and density estimates 
(Habib et al. 2012), with a factor of 95% applied to moose density and population estimates. 
 
Results 
There were 554 white-tailed deer observed in 85 groups. Of the 554 white-tailed deer observed, 117 (21%) were 
bucks, 259 (47%) were does, 162 (29%) were fawns and 16 (3%) were not classified. The buck: doe ratio was 
0.45 and the fawn: doe ratio was 0.63 (Table 1). The average white-tailed deer density was estimated at 1.46 
individuals/km2. Population was estimated at 2002 (Table 1); 435 bucks, 964 does and 603 fawns.  
 
There were 196 mule deer observed within 30 groups. Of the 196 mule deer identified 48 (24%) were bucks, 97 
(49%) were does, 51 (26%) were fawns and 0 (0%) were not classified. The buck: doe ratio was 0.49 and the fawn: 
doe ratio was 0.53 (Table 2). The average mule deer density was estimated at 0.46 individuals/km2. Population 
was estimated at 634 (Table 2); 155 bucks, 314 does and 165 fawns. 
 
There were 39 moose observed within 11 groups. Of the 39 moose identified, 13 (33%) were bulls, 13 (33%) were 
cows, 13 (33%) were calves and 0 (0%) were not classified. The bull:cow ratio was 1.00 and the calf:cow ratio was 
1.00 (Table 3). The average moose density was estimated at 0.06 individuals/km 2. Population was estimated at 86 
(Table 3); 29 bulls, 29 cows and 29 calves. 
No elk were observed during the survey. 
We also observed 63 coyotes, 20 Sharp-tailed grouse, 20 Grey partridge, 1 red fox, 1 porcupine, and 60 snow 
buntings. These are incidental observations only and should not be considered minimum total counts.
